title: 07 — Excel Templates
html:
07 — Excel Templates

The one idea: let a designer own the look of the report in Excel, and let code own the numbers. The template holds styles, formulas, charts and named cells around an empty Excel table. Code opens it, fills that table from a DataFrame, resizes it, and saves a copy. The template itself is never changed.

1. What it is

Piece Role
Template .xlsx Made in Excel by whoever owns the report: title, logo, styles, an Excel table with the header row plus one styled sample row, formulas and charts that refer to the table
Named cells (defined names) Places code writes single values, e.g. ReportDate
openpyxl Opens an existing workbook, writes values, resizes the table, saves a new file
Polars Builds the exact DataFrame to load: column names equal to the table headers, rounded money

Why openpyxl and not write_excel: XlsxWriter (behind write_excel) can only create workbooks. Filling a template means editing one.

---
title: Template-driven Excel reports
---
flowchart LR
    D["Designer's template<br/>(styles, table, formulas, charts)"] --> F["fill_table()"]
    P["Polars query<br/>(columns = table headers)"] --> F
    F --> O["report_2026-11-07.xlsx"]
    O --> X["Excel recalculates<br/>formulas on open"]

2. Why it matters

  • Report layouts change often. With a template, a layout change is an Excel edit, not a code change.
  • Formatting by code (colours, widths, fonts) is long and fragile. Copying the template's style is one line.
  • Formulas and charts in the template keep working because they point at the table, which grows to fit the data.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Design rules for templates

  1. Put the data in an Excel table with a fixed name (Holdings). Formulas use structured references (Holdings[value]), which follow the table as it grows.
  2. Leave one styled sample row under the header. Code copies its style to every row.
  3. Use defined names for single values (ReportDate), not hard-coded cell addresses.
  4. Keep totals above or beside the table, not under it, so a growing table never overwrites them.

3.2 The fill steps

  1. load_workbook(template), then find the table by name.
  2. Check the DataFrame's columns equal the table's headers. Refuse if not.
  3. Write values row by row, copying the sample row's style.
  4. Set table.ref to the new size.
  5. Write named values.
  6. Set wb.calculation.fullCalcOnLoad = True, because openpyxl doesn't calculate formulas, so Excel must on open.
  7. Save under a new name.

3.3 Check what survives a save

openpyxl rebuilds the file when it saves, and doesn't support every Excel feature. In this test (openpyxl 3.1.5), tables, a chart, data validation, defined names and conditional formatting all survived. Check each new template. Macros need .xlsm with keep_vba=True, and some features (for example slicers, form controls, pivot caches from external data) may not survive. The check script in section 4.2 lists anything lost.

4. Working code

4.1 Fill a template

The script builds a stand-in template (in practice you open the designer's file), fills its Holdings table from a Polars aggregation, sets the report date, and checks the result.

from copy import copy
from datetime import date
import openpyxl
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill
from openpyxl.utils import get_column_letter, range_boundaries
from openpyxl.worksheet.table import Table, TableStyleInfo
import polars as pl

# --- A stand-in for the template a designer would hand you (normally you just open their file). ---
def make_template(path):
    wb = openpyxl.Workbook(); ws = wb.active; ws.title = "Report"
    ws["A1"], ws["A1"].font = "Fund holdings as of", Font(bold=True, size=14)
    ws["B1"].number_format = "dd-mmm-yyyy"
    wb.defined_names["ReportDate"] = openpyxl.workbook.defined_name.DefinedName("ReportDate", attr_text="Report!$B$1")
    ws["D1"], ws["E1"] = "Total value", "=SUBTOTAL(109,Holdings[value])"
    ws["E1"].number_format = "#,##0"
    for col, header in enumerate(["fund_id", "category", "trades", "value"], start=1):
        ws.cell(3, col, header)
    styles = ["0", "@", "#,##0", "#,##0.00"]                      # the one styled sample row
    for col, fmt in enumerate(styles, start=1):
        cell = ws.cell(4, col); cell.number_format = fmt
        cell.fill = PatternFill("solid", fgColor="EAF1FB")
    table = Table(displayName="Holdings", ref="A3:D4")
    table.tableStyleInfo = TableStyleInfo(name="TableStyleMedium2", showRowStripes=True)
    ws.add_table(table)
    wb.save(path)

# --- The reusable part: fill a named Excel table in a template from a DataFrame. ---
def fill_table(template, output, sheet, table_name, df, named_values=None):
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(template)
    ws = wb[sheet]
    table = ws.tables[table_name]
    min_col, min_row, max_col, _ = range_boundaries(table.ref)
    headers = [ws.cell(min_row, c).value for c in range(min_col, max_col + 1)]
    if headers != df.columns:
        raise ValueError(f"template columns {headers} != data columns {df.columns}")
    style_row = [ws.cell(min_row + 1, c) for c in range(min_col, max_col + 1)]
    for r, row in enumerate(df.iter_rows(), start=min_row + 1):
        for c, (value, template_cell) in enumerate(zip(row, style_row), start=min_col):
            cell = ws.cell(r, c, value)
            cell._style = copy(template_cell._style)            # number format, fill, font, border
    last_row = min_row + max(df.height, 1)
    table.ref = f"{get_column_letter(min_col)}{min_row}:{get_column_letter(max_col)}{last_row}"
    for name, value in (named_values or {}).items():
        sheet_name, coord = next(iter(wb.defined_names[name].destinations))
        wb[sheet_name][coord.replace("$", "")] = value
    wb.calculation.fullCalcOnLoad = True                       # openpyxl stores formulas; Excel calculates them
    wb.save(output)

make_template("data/holdings_template.xlsx")
holdings = (
    pl.read_parquet("data/trades.parquet")
    .group_by("fund_id", "category")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("trades"), pl.col("amount").sum().round(2).alias("value"))   # round money
    .sort("value", descending=True)
    .with_columns(pl.col("category").cast(pl.String), pl.col("trades").cast(pl.Int64))
)
fill_table("data/holdings_template.xlsx", "data/holdings_2026-11-07.xlsx", "Report", "Holdings",
           holdings, named_values={"ReportDate": date(2026, 11, 7)})

# Check the result: data, table size, formatting on the last row, formula left for Excel.
back = pl.read_excel("data/holdings_2026-11-07.xlsx", table_name="Holdings")
print("rows written:", back.height, "| equal to source:", back.equals(holdings))
ws = openpyxl.load_workbook("data/holdings_2026-11-07.xlsx")["Report"]
last = ws.cell(3 + holdings.height, 4)
print("table ref:", ws.tables["Holdings"].ref, "| last value cell format:", last.number_format,
      "| fill:", last.fill.fgColor.rgb)
print("B1:", ws["B1"].value.date(), "| E1 formula:", ws["E1"].value)
try:
    fill_table("data/holdings_template.xlsx", "data/bad.xlsx", "Report", "Holdings", holdings.drop("trades"))
except ValueError as err:
    print("refused:", err)

Output:

rows written: 50 | equal to source: True
table ref: A3:D53 | last value cell format: #,##0.00 | fill: 00EAF1FB
B1: 2026-11-07 | E1 formula: =SUBTOTAL(109,Holdings[value])
refused: template columns ['fund_id', 'category', 'trades', 'value'] != data columns ['fund_id', 'category', 'value']

What to notice:

  • The table grew from one sample row to 50 rows (A3:D53). The last row carries the template's number format and fill.
  • The total formula is untouched. It refers to Holdings[value], so Excel totals all 50 rows on open.
  • A DataFrame missing a column was refused before anything was written.
  • Money is rounded to 2 places before writing. Without it, the round-trip check failed on the last digits of parallel float sums (04, section 3.4).

4.2 Check a template survives openpyxl

import sys, zipfile
import openpyxl

# Round-trip check for a template: open and save it with openpyxl, then compare what is inside.
# Run it once on every new template before building a report on it.
def parts(path):
    keep = ("chart", "table", "drawing", "pivot", "vbaProject", "media", "slicer", "externalLink")
    return sorted(n for n in zipfile.ZipFile(path).namelist() if any(k in n for k in keep))

template = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "data/holdings_template.xlsx"
openpyxl.load_workbook(template).save("data/roundtrip.xlsx")
before, after = parts(template), parts("data/roundtrip.xlsx")
print("inside the template:", before)
print("lost on save:", sorted(set(before) - set(after)) or "nothing")

Output (for the template above; run it with your own file's path):

inside the template: ['xl/tables/table1.xml']
lost on save: nothing

5. Common mistakes

  1. Writing into the template file itself instead of saving a copy.
  2. Hard-coded cell addresses (ws["C17"]) instead of a table and defined names.
  3. Not resizing the table, so filters, banding and formulas stop at the old last row.
  4. Totals placed under the table, overwritten when the data grows.
  5. Expecting openpyxl to calculate formulas. It stores them, and Excel calculates them.
  6. Skipping the round-trip check on a template with macros, slicers or pivots.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. In Excel, add a column chart on Holdings[value] to the template, refill it from code, and confirm the chart covers all rows.
  2. Extend fill_table to fill two tables on two sheets from two DataFrames.
  3. Add a guard that refuses more rows than a limit you choose, with a clear message.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why can't write_excel fill a template?
  2. Why should the data area be an Excel table?
  3. How does the code keep the template's formatting on new rows?
  4. Why set fullCalcOnLoad?
  5. What should you check before trusting a new template?

Answers

  1. It uses XlsxWriter, which only creates new workbooks.
  2. Tables give a name to target, structured references that follow the data, and filters and banding for free.
  3. It copies the style of the template's sample row into every written cell.
  4. openpyxl doesn't calculate formulas, so Excel should recalculate everything when the file opens.
  5. That opening and saving it with openpyxl loses nothing (run the round-trip check).
